name: PCB Lead Time

claims.claim_text: For most circuit board fabrication the price-defining variable is turnaround time rather than board complexity, layer count, hole count or the geography of the fab; a board wanted tomorrow costs a great deal and the same board wanted in two months costs almost nothing.
claims.quote_verbatim: for most, uh, circuit board manufacturing, the defining characteristic is actually like a turnaround time
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: Very complex boards can be obtained for almost no money if the buyer accepts a two-month wait, so the ordering interface for prototype fabrication is best framed as a price-versus-time slider rather than a specification.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can get a crazy, crazy complex board in two months for almost no money.
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: For prototype boards the purchasing criteria are cost and lead time, with quality treated as almost secondary.
claims.quote_verbatim: with PCB, it's all about lead time and price
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: Fabrication lead time and delivery must be sequenced before assembly in a project schedule, because the board cannot be built until it physically exists; arranging a contract manufacturer alone takes five to ten days, which can rule out outsourcing on a short deadline and force an in-house build.
claims.quote_verbatim: it takes five or 10 days just to arrange that
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LED Designs, Last Minute Designs and Board Designs

claims.claim_text: On a build with roughly ten days available, the schedule was met by fabricating bare boards overnight in Taiwan because no local fabricator was fast enough, and by hand-building twenty assemblies in house.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't build the board unless you physically have it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LED Designs, Last Minute Designs and Board Designs

claims.claim_text: The same four-layer board can be quoted at a twelve-day standard turn, an eight-day expedited turn, or a one-day turn costing on the order of a thousand dollars, so the turn selected is the dominant term in the price.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's a 12 day turn for a four layer board
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LED Designs, Last Minute Designs and Board Designs

claims.claim_text: Twenty-four-hour turns on multilayer boards were bought at two to three thousand dollars apiece in commercial practice, and an eight-layer board in twenty-four hours sits at the edge of what is physically achievable, requiring every material step to go perfectly.
claims.quote_verbatim: sometimes we would pay, you know, two, $3,000 to get a board turned in 24 hours
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: An eight-layer board turned in twenty-four hours is at the limit of what the process can deliver and leaves no margin for a materials problem.
claims.quote_verbatim: to make an eight-layer board in 24 hours is practically, you know, it's beyond the limits of human capability
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Space Bound, Again - Xtreme Xtraplanetary Xenonosocomiophobia

claims.claim_text: Paying an expedite premium is justified only by a demonstrable downstream need for the board on that date; expediting because the work feels urgent produces the common outcome of having paid for speed that was never used.
claims.quote_verbatim: the justification should always be that if you're paying for an eight layer board overnight, it's like, you have a need for it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: PCB Mills, SDR and Oscilloscopes - Flaunting Furbelow Fanciness

claims.claim_text: The characteristic waste in expedited fabrication is discovering after delivery that the schedule would have tolerated the standard turn.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's the worst when you pay it and then you're like, oh, I guess I could have waited.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Domestic quick-turn assembly houses charge a large premium — on the order of three thousand dollars above parts cost for a three-day job — because meeting the date requires displacing other customers' jobs on the line.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's going to be like three grand on top of the actual parts
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The mechanism behind the expedite premium is queue displacement: the expedited job is inserted ahead of other work already scheduled.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because they bump other people's jobs.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Batch or panel-pooling fabrication services place a submitted design into whatever spare space the next scheduled panel has, so the quoted turnaround is not a firm commitment but a function of when that panel runs.
claims.quote_verbatim: they just throw your design onto the next batch that goes through any spare space
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Bob Widlar, Electronic Design, FIRST Robotics - Monday, Meta Monday

claims.claim_text: A pooled-panel service placed boards on a panel the same day they were submitted and delivered in about two weeks typically; sitting on the most commonly ordered panel option, such as the standard two-layer board share, moves an order through faster than an unusual specification.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're on the most common part of a board share, then you'll obviously move up faster
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Fake it till you make it

claims.claim_text: Low-cost Chinese fabricators also pool customer designs onto shared panels, but do so silently, quoting a board price rather than disclosing the board share.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of the cheap PCB factories in China, they board share, but you don't know it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Fake it till you make it

claims.claim_text: A pooled-panel service operating from United States fabs reported an average order-to-shipment time of eight days, putting boards in a domestic customer's hands in roughly ten days with priority shipping.
claims.quote_verbatim: my average order to shipping time is now eight days
claims.speaker: Laen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: That service chose domestic fabs over Chinese ones on speed and quality: Chinese fabrication then meant waiting a month or more, with roughly one board in four failing.
claims.quote_verbatim: we had a pretty high failure rate of about one in four
claims.speaker: Laen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: Matching a seven-day domestic delivery through a Chinese fab requires buying a three-day turn and overnight shipping, which erodes the nominal cost advantage of offshore fabrication.
claims.quote_verbatim: If I wanted them back in the seven days that I currently do, that I currently get them back, then I'm paying for three-day turn times in China.
claims.speaker: Laen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: Turnaround should be quoted in calendar days rather than business days, because business-day definitions are renegotiated once an order is running late; one fabrication service adopted a twelve calendar day turn for that reason.
claims.quote_verbatim: one of our peeves is, is working days
claims.speaker: Jonathan Hirschman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Hirschman of PCB:NG

claims.claim_text: A business-day turn placed just before a weekend absorbs the non-working days as well, so a three-day turn ordered on a Saturday delivers no sooner than one ordered on the following Monday.
claims.quote_verbatim: I put in my order on a Saturday and I'm like, oh, yay, three day turn
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A contract assembler's low-cost service ran fifteen business days, with a five-day service priced higher because both the bare boards and the components have to be expedited to hold that date.
claims.quote_verbatim: our standard service is 15 business days and that's what we call our low-cost service
claims.speaker: Chris Church
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: Specifying an exact calculated component value rather than a range can force a part with a twenty-week lead time; a quoting system that suggests in-range substitutes where no specific part number is mandated removes that self-inflicted delay.
claims.quote_verbatim: And you can only get it on 20 week lead time.
claims.speaker: Chris Church
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: An integrated quote-and-build service delivered a board three days from the completion of design, which is unattainable through a traditional contract manufacturer because a conventional CM cannot return a quote within an hour.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's not possible with a traditional CM because they can't turn a quote in, in an hour
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: One quick-turn assembly service shipped about eighty-one percent of orders placed on its fastest lead time within roughly three days of file upload, covering fabrication, assembly and everything required to get the order out of the door.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's about 81% of our orders that are ordered on our fastest lead time ship within about three days
claims.episode_title: CircuitHub, 12 Years Later with Andrew Seddon

claims.claim_text: Conventional electronics manufacturing services carry two to three month order lead times, and complex programmable parts have been seen at six to twelve month delivery because the distributor places the order with the semiconductor fab only on demand; meanwhile the rest of the bill of materials accumulates at the assembler as tied-up cash.
claims.quote_verbatim: you place your order with the distributor and then the distributor places the order with the semiconductor fab, and then it takes six months to make them
claims.episode_title: CircuitHub, 12 Years Later with Andrew Seddon

claims.claim_text: A single missing component halts an entire assembled board, making a stalled order a visible physical manifestation of trapped cash on the production line.
claims.quote_verbatim: if that one part's not there, it sits, it waits
claims.episode_title: CircuitHub, 12 Years Later with Andrew Seddon

claims.claim_text: Where engineering hours are expensive, buying fast board and mechanical prototype turns is the cheaper option overall, because the hours saved waiting exceed the expedite fee and clients optimising for time to market value it directly.
claims.quote_verbatim: it aligned best with their goals to not, to not sit and spin your wheels waiting for PCBs to come back in three weeks when you could turn them in five days
claims.speaker: Kerry Scharfglass

claims.claim_text: Consulting practice is to obtain client approval before spending client money on expedited turnaround, telling them in advance what the acceleration will cost so the expense can be authorised rather than discovered.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've never spent client money without permission
claims.speaker: Dave Young

claims.claim_text: A client's choice of the low-cost assembly route commits the consultant to roughly a month before boards return, which has to be sequenced against other clients' work rather than treated as idle time.
claims.quote_verbatim: they wanted to go macro fab. So I've got like a month before it's going to come back
claims.speaker: Dave Young

claims.claim_text: Collecting boards in person from a nearby fabricator saves a business day, and in a startup schedule one business day can translate into three real days of delivered outcome.
claims.quote_verbatim: in the startup world, one business day could very easily mean three real days
claims.speaker: Dave Young

claims.claim_text: Any query raised during fabrication adds about two days to delivery, because the exchange crosses time zones and each round trip costs most of a working day at each end.
claims.quote_verbatim: any such issue that comes up, you can add two days to the time
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A fabricator's upload preview that renders only top and bottom copper regardless of the stack-up will not flag missing inner-layer files, so the omission surfaces a day later as an email from the fab and costs a further day or two across time zones.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can lose a day or two with time zones.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: With low-cost offshore fabrication the dominant term in delivered lead time is shipping rather than fabrication, with express shipping available as the lever; two-dollar boards were arriving in five days.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's really just the shipping that takes a long time.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Customs clearance is an unpredictable component of delivered lead time that cannot be committed to a customer: the same importer saw shipments cleared in seven days on some occasions and seven weeks on others.
claims.quote_verbatim: Sometimes we are able to get our shipments cleared in seven days. Sometimes it takes seven weeks.
claims.speaker: Pallav Aggarwal

claims.claim_text: A change in customs inspection policy can add delay to an established route without any change at the fabricator; a batch service that shipped three days after order took about a week in transit from Hong Kong, extended by newly increased inspection of packages from that origin.
claims.quote_verbatim: there are more inspecting packages from Hong Kong
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Bob Widlar, Electronic Design, FIRST Robotics - Monday, Meta Monday

claims.claim_text: Carrier disruption is a schedule risk independent of the distributor or fabricator, and there is no practical recourse: a two-day distributor delivery ran to six days through a courier failure, and a weather event at a courier hub cost a week beyond the one day announced.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm currently on day six of waiting for a two day delivery from DigiKey.
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: Small Scale Electronics Manufacturing with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: Unannounced carrier delays break every downstream schedule that was built on the promised transit time.
claims.quote_verbatim: That screws up all the schedules.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Paying for an expedited turn does not guarantee it: a high-specification board at four-mil trace and space with a BGA, bought at a three-to-four-day turn for around ten thousand dollars, arrived in four weeks, while a parallel low-cost order placed as a hedge arrived first and was used instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: four mil trace space BGA and paid for like, you know, three or four day turn
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: Small Scale Electronics Manufacturing with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: Where a hard date depends on an expedited board, placing a low-cost order in parallel provides a fallback that costs little relative to the expedite fee.
claims.quote_verbatim: the four weeks versus four days
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: Small Scale Electronics Manufacturing with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: Receiving and validating components in hand before releasing the board to assembly costs about two days up front and avoids losing two weeks at the back end, which is what a re-spin costs when the assembler discovers a part was never in the kit.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's better to burn two days up front than lose two weeks on the back end
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A nominal four-day fabrication turn from a Chinese board house amounts to a solid two weeks once shipping is counted, and a re-spin adds another two weeks to that cycle.
claims.quote_verbatim: even if I'm using a, you know, a board house that has a four day turn with shipping from China, it's like, okay, that's a solid two weeks
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Even a perfectly sequenced prototype cycle carries about a two-week wait unless hundreds of dollars in rush charges are paid, because the logistics of ordering parts, fabricating and shipping cannot be compressed further at standard rates.
claims.quote_verbatim: best case scenario you got you line everything up and you still got a two-week wait unless you're paying you know hundreds of dollars rush charges
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: We'll Believe It When We See It - Hiring Hypercatalectic Helpelp

claims.claim_text: A two-week wait has a cost beyond the schedule: motivation for the project decays across the gap and the work is deferred in favour of whatever is currently in front of the engineer.
claims.quote_verbatim: your enthusiasm can die in that time
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: We'll Believe It When We See It - Hiring Hypercatalectic Helpelp

claims.claim_text: Boards that arrive after the design has already moved on are wasted: a five-week delivery arrived after the design had been revised, so the boards were never built up.
claims.quote_verbatim: by the time they took, what, five weeks to get here, I'd already figured, oh, no, I want to change things, and there was no point building it up
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A fabrication service whose demand outgrows its capacity begins to miss its own published turnaround: an eight-day standard turn that had been met reliably slipped as volume grew, and prices were raised to bring demand back into balance with capacity.
claims.quote_verbatim: they used to have like an eight-day, that would be their standard turnaround, eight days
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A two-layer prototype board at around ninety dollars on a claimed four-day turnaround was the going quick-turn offer from small regional fabricators in the early 2010s.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's pretty good, and they do it in four days.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Pooled low-cost fabrication was quoted at four to six cents per square inch plus roughly a hundred dollars of tooling, with a claimed three to four day turnaround, making the tooling charge rather than the board area the dominant cost on a prototype.
claims.quote_verbatim: from four to six cents, plus a hundred bucks, you know, tooling
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Chinese fabricators and component suppliers close for roughly two weeks over Chinese New Year, and the shutdown routinely catches projects that resumed on schedule after the western new year.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's Chinese New Year, and, you know, you just get caught short, and you always forget about it.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Western board houses shut for a couple of weeks over Christmas and the new year; on an offshore order the same shutdown is absorbed into an already long lead time and is less visible.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you use the Western ones, yeah, they'll shut down for a couple of weeks
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: FPGA, Xess, 32 Bit - Quirky Qualitative Questions

claims.claim_text: A job that would ordinarily take about a month cannot be planned as a month when it spans both the western holidays and Chinese New Year, because suppliers on both sides are absent for part of the window.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can get stuff done in a month, but when it's over Christmas and new year's
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Regional supply disruption recovers unevenly between fabricators rather than uniformly across a country, so capacity has to be checked per vendor: during one disruption some houses were delivering normally while others quoted eight weeks, and a four-to-five-day service moved out to ten days.
claims.quote_verbatim: Depends on who the manufacturer is though.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Board shipments continued out of a locked-down manufacturing region with roughly one to two weeks of added delay rather than stopping altogether.
claims.quote_verbatim: his stuff is about a week or two delayed, but it was still getting out
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: When a disruption is announced after an order has already gone out, the decision to make immediately is what the real in-house deadline for the boards is and what cost tolerance exists for working around it; the alternative is to accept delivery whenever it comes.
claims.quote_verbatim: what is my real deadline on boards in house
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Just-in-time supply is sound only while lead times stay bounded; the model fails outright when lead times stretch towards a year.
claims.quote_verbatim: Just in time is a great concept until you, you know, when it stops working.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Hardware iteration cycles run to weeks or months to get a board back, worse where shipping distances are long, and almost no automated checking is done before committing to fabrication; schematic checks run at commit time would be the hardware counterpart to software unit tests.
claims.quote_verbatim: we have iteration cycle of, you know, weeks or months to get your PCB back
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: The compile-and-test cycle for a board is measured in weeks depending on what is paid, which is why deliberate flexibility has to be designed in before the data is released rather than added afterwards.
claims.quote_verbatim: compile time on a PCB is about what? You know, three weeks.
claims.episode_title: What defines an engineer? - Job Judging Jeremiad

claims.claim_text: Remote manufacturing lengthens the feedback loop on subtle board faults such as a trace changing capacitance or resistance, because the lead time governs how long it takes for such errors to return to the designer.
claims.quote_verbatim: the lead time on, on when those errors come back to you
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Melbourne, Hackerspace & Calibration - Vacuuous Vortex Verification

claims.claim_text: Milling boards in house turned a single-sided board around in about twenty minutes and a double-sided board in about an hour, against a week or two from a fabrication shop; the value taken from it was the number of design iterations attempted, not the boards themselves.
claims.quote_verbatim: mill it, you know, 20 minutes later
claims.speaker: Mike Grover

claims.claim_text: The decision rule for in-house board fabrication is a learning-rate one: the machine earns its place when it compresses months of iteration into days, not when it beats the per-board price.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you can compress six months of learning into two days, then that's when the mill's worth it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The financial form of the same decision is a crossover calculation: divide the cost of the machine by the cost of the expedited boards it would displace and establish how soon the crossover occurs before buying.
claims.quote_verbatim: take the cost of the machine. Look at the cost of however many overnight boards you can get for that. Same cost. And how soon are you going to do the crossover

claims.claim_text: A vendor of benchtop assembly equipment published a return-on-investment calculator for that crossover, with the qualifying question being how much pain a ten-day wait for boards causes rather than the headline machine price.
claims.quote_verbatim: is waiting 10 days to get boards back a huge pain in the butt
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: In-house milling is justified in narrow cases — largely ground-plane RF boards, in-house rapid prototypes, or runs of about ten boards — because commercially fabricated boards are cheap and fast enough to win elsewhere.
claims.quote_verbatim: a real PCB is just so cheap and fast these days
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: An in-house etching setup is worth having only if it is kept permanently ready, since the difference between tanks standing by and equipment that has to be unpacked decides whether it gets used; in practice it serves simple boards such as breakouts, with a local fabricator covering anything else in two to four days.
claims.quote_verbatim: if he's not busy, I can get him good by 11, and he'll ship out the same day

claims.claim_text: Same-day in-house board production earns its place where hands-on user-experience testing is needed, since that testing cannot begin until a physical board exists; the case was stronger when quick-batch boards in Australia cost around a hundred dollars rather than twenty.
claims.quote_verbatim: the quick batch boards you could actually get in Australia were like a hundred bucks, not 20 bucks
claims.speaker: Ariel Briner
claims.episode_title: An interview with Ariel Briner of Cartesian Co

claims.claim_text: A weekly prototype cadence was run by pairing a three-day board turn with same-week parts and stencil supply: Gerber data out Friday evening to United States fabs that work weekends, parts ordered Monday for overnight delivery, a locally cut stencil in hours, and the pick-and-place programmed Tuesday morning so five to ten populated boards existed by Tuesday evening.
claims.quote_verbatim: We would send the board Gerber data out on a Friday evening. We would have the board spun on a three-day turnaround
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: Fabricators that work through the weekend are what make a Friday-to-Tuesday prototype cycle possible.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's a lot of board companies in the U.S. that work over the weekend.
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: Two routes were maintained deliberately in parallel by one practitioner: a pooled low-cost service at one to two weeks for hobby and low-priority work, and a domestic fab at five to seven hundred dollars for overnight or two-day turnaround on high-priority work, with the choice made per job rather than per shop.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'll pay $500 or $700 and get, you know, overnight or two day turnaround
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: A hand-assembly house returned a populated box of boards in under two weeks from the point at which parts were drop-shipped and inspected boards sent, including weather disruption; hand-placing 0402 parts under a microscope carries a large surcharge over machine placement.
claims.quote_verbatim: we had less than a two-week turnaround between when we drop-shipped the parts to our assembly house
claims.speaker: Ian Danaher
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Daniher - Nascent Nonolith Numquid

claims.claim_text: A quick-turn prototype assembly quote of five boards at twelve hundred dollars plus parts, shipping in three days, illustrates the going rate for compressing fabrication and assembly into a single short turn.
claims.quote_verbatim: Five boards, $1,200 plus parts, ships in three days.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Adding layers costs both money and schedule: moving from four to six layers adds an extra day or two, and on most projects the time is the more expensive of the two.
claims.quote_verbatim: It is an extra day or two, which is often, you know, time is the most expensive thing.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The cost and time of a prototype board fell from weeks and thousands of dollars in the late 2000s to under a week and about fifty dollars, but hardware still has no zero-marginal-cost retry in the way software does.
claims.quote_verbatim: 10, 15 years ago, it might've been weeks and thousands of dollars. Now, you know, you'll get a board from JLCPCB in less than a week for 50 bucks.
claims.speaker: Sergiy Nesterenko

claims.claim_text: Cheap fast iteration carries an unpriced externality in electronic waste, which is part of the argument for spending simulation effort instead of respins where high-speed or high-reliability requirements already justify the solver cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: unstated negative externalities like e-waste
claims.speaker: Sergiy Nesterenko

claims.claim_text: Cheap fast fabrication changed what a failed board costs: submitting a design once meant waiting months and paying hundreds or thousands before discovering an error, whereas affordable failure is what makes exploratory design viable.
claims.quote_verbatim: you wait for months, you pay hundreds of bucks, maybe thousands. And then you discover like after you submitted
claims.speaker: Bitluni

claims.claim_text: In 1980 a sub-eight-hour turn on a two-layer board of about three by two inches cost around fifteen hundred dollars, equivalent to roughly six thousand dollars later.
claims.quote_verbatim: we got less than an eight-hour turn on those PC boards. And in 1980, that cost like $1,500 a PC board
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Bil Herd - Zany Z80 Zygology

claims.claim_text: Before prototype fabrication services existed, a board cost eight hundred to a thousand dollars and took two weeks, on top of an internal paper purchase requisition process, which is why in-house etching that produced a board the same day was treated as a revolution inside companies.
claims.quote_verbatim: it'd cost you 800 or a thousand bucks to get your board made. It'd take two weeks.

claims.claim_text: Before online distribution, local distributors carried no stock and quoted lead times as long as forty weeks for ordinary parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: 40 weeks lead time, sir
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Supply Chain Woes And Wares - Nonplussed Neotechnic Nithing

claims.claim_text: The classic forty-week semiconductor lead time reflects a build that starts from bare wafers rather than from stock.
claims.quote_verbatim: that lead time represents, it's, they're starting with bare wafers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A vendor whose parts sample freely but ship on forty-week lead times becomes a design-in hazard, and several large companies responded with a blanket internal rule against using that manufacturer's parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was actually a blanket rule at many big companies
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: BASIC, Chip companies & Robots - Pernicious Projects, Puppies in Peril

claims.claim_text: Restarting a semiconductor fab after a shutdown takes long enough that part lead times ran thirty to forty weeks afterwards, which is why high-volume design requires parts with second and third sources rather than parts that are merely available today.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to have parts that have to choose parts that have a second source and a third source
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Genuine second sourcing has become harder because packaging and footprints differ between manufacturers and are themselves protected; where no pin-compatible alternative exists, the available escape is often a higher-performance part from the same manufacturer, bought at a higher price to avoid a three-month wait.
claims.quote_verbatim: you may be able to get out of the shit by buying the higher performance part
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Ceramic capacitors & High end scopes - Kempt Kickstarter Kakorrhaphiophobia

claims.claim_text: A part that is cheap and in stock may be cheap because stock is being cleared ahead of end of life; manufacturers schedule production from demand trends, so a part on a declining trend is precisely the one that later returns a twelve-week lead time.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's when you're going to get hit with your 12-week lead time
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Risky Components and Hardware Innovation - Slipshod Shack Shutdown

claims.claim_text: Distributor stock is not reserved: a part checked as in stock can be gone between the check and the order, converting an off-the-shelf part into a twelve-week lead time.
claims.quote_verbatim: They were in stock in DigiKey yesterday, but you went to press the order button today and the stock is zero.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Quantities should be quoted early, because crossing the distributor's stock threshold moves the order to the manufacturer and brings manufacturer lead times and minimum order quantities with it.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you cross that threshold, 800 number 801 means you have to order from the manufacturer and then you are dealing with lead times and minimum order quantities
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Key long-lead components are bought before the money for the build arrives when a campaign or order is pending, because parts costed at design time can be taken by another buyer in the interval, leaving the project holding a design it cannot build for twelve weeks.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I've had to snap up some of these key parts. Otherwise, I knew I'd be left holding the bag because some of them are 12 weeks lead time.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Funding New/Manufacturing Old Projects - Radical Robotic Requisition

claims.claim_text: At volume the lead time has to be designed in from the start: fifty light-emitting diodes on fifty thousand units cannot be sourced casually, carries at least a twenty-week lead time, and once half a million parts are committed the part can no longer be changed, so thermal and other qualification has to be complete before the order is placed.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is going to be a very specific lead time. It's at least 20 weeks
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A component ordering rule can be automated only once it is stated explicitly — a reorder threshold set so that the replenishment arrives before stock runs out given the lead time — whereas the rule most commonly applied in practice remains an unstated judgement.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you can say such a form, such a rule, then you can automate it, you can program it, and the system can do it
claims.speaker: Andreas Spiess

claims.claim_text: Build-to-order finished goods carry reorder lead times of about two months because the supplier holds no stock, so stock-out planning has to run two months ahead of demand.
claims.quote_verbatim: what's the lead time? Two months.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Distributors began shipping partial quantities against orders — a hundred delivered against five hundred ordered, with the balance uncertain — so component tracking has to model split shipments and revised delivery estimates rather than a single receipt.
claims.quote_verbatim: you order 500 of a part and they will only ship you 100

claims.claim_text: A small manufacturer ordering an eclectic mix of parts through distributors encountered lead times as long as sixty-two weeks during the shortage period.
claims.quote_verbatim: I can't get a 62 weeks on a lead time.

claims.claim_text: Parts in specialised footprints have no substitution path when they become unavailable, so the only remaining response is to redesign them out of the board.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not like these are footprint drop in place, replacements
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: During the 2021 shortage even basic through-hole components such as standard indicator light-emitting diodes took three to four months to obtain.
claims.quote_verbatim: it took about probably three or four months to get those parts
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Component vendors whose minimum interesting order is around a million units quote both high prices and long lead times — eighteen weeks in one case — for ten-thousand-unit orders, so ordering in small batches to control cash makes the pricing worse.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's, it's going to take 18 weeks
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: After a successful demonstration, the honest answer to when another unit can be built is the component lead time plus the debug time on the boards already made, which is why prototypes assembled from parts scavenged off other products create an interval in which the product cannot be reproduced.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's like 12 weeks plus however long it takes us to debug those 10 boards
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Lead-time management cannot be delegated to a turnkey assembler; availability has to be considered while the product is being designed.
claims.quote_verbatim: You've got to think about this while you're designing the product.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Spacing Out On Space - Dave's Dongle Designing

claims.claim_text: A known eight-week minimum lead time is useful precisely because it is a hard constraint that resource planning cannot negotiate away.
claims.quote_verbatim: we know eight-week minimum lead time, you're not getting around that, that is very useful
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Don't Turn It On, Don't Take It Apart

claims.claim_text: Whether a part can be bought in production quantity, not whether a few are in stock, decides if it can be designed in: five units at a distributor are no help against a build of ten thousand facing a forty-week lead time.
claims.quote_verbatim: that doesn't help you when you want to build 10,000 of them and there's a 40-week lead time
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Pre-purchasing every long-lead part is possible with enough planning horizon, and remains necessary because alternatives exist for most parts but a single unobtainable one stops the build.
claims.quote_verbatim: it only takes that one and you're screwed
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Manufacturer advisories are a usable early warning: one letter advised customers to expect lead times stretching from a familiar two to four weeks out to six to eight weeks or more and to place orders immediately, and orders placed that week were quoted delivery two months out.
claims.quote_verbatim: expect lead times sort of six to eight weeks and even more for some projects
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Harrison - X-ray Examining Xenogogue

claims.claim_text: The schedule risk in project work often sits before the work starts rather than in the build: the interval between a proposal and the decision to proceed consumes the slack, and the accumulated urgency is then paid for in one-week board turns and couriers.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's the time between someone actually saying, yes, this is how we're going to do it.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Harrison - X-ray Examining Xenogogue

claims.claim_text: A fabricator can be asked to split a production run against a hard date: one supplier accepted a customer-supplied partial reel, ran a hundred and twenty of five hundred boards immediately to meet a delivery commitment, and completed the balance on standard lead time without charging for the split.
claims.quote_verbatim: they ran 120 boards for me
claims.speaker: Zach Fredin

claims.claim_text: Where lead times will not meet a committed date, saying so explicitly to the supplier is what opens the possibility of a partial run.
claims.quote_verbatim: these lead times aren't going to work
claims.speaker: Zach Fredin

claims.claim_text: In an electronic design automation vendor's in-house hardware group, large eight-layer prototype boards costing thousands of dollars each were ordered freely and sometimes turned in twenty-four hours at double or triple the standard price, on the reasoning that a new concept could then be spun quickly.
claims.quote_verbatim: we would get boards prototype, like they were candy

claims.claim_text: Long lead times shape the process a designer chooses, not just the schedule: overseas on-demand machining at a couple of weeks biases work towards parts that can be printed in house.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's going to take a couple of weeks to arrive to me because like a lot of the really cheap online services are overseas in China
claims.speaker: Aaed Musa

claims.claim_text: Iteration speed differs by roughly two orders of magnitude between board work and packaging work: a packaging house takes about three months to return parts where a board fabricator returns boards in about three days.
claims.quote_verbatim: a packaging house will easily take you three months to get stuff back from them

claims.claim_text: Custom silicon schedules slip against fixed external dates in a way board schedules do not: one design returned in mid-October to November against an August expectation, which matters when the deliverable is tied to a conference or a graduation date.
claims.quote_verbatim: we got our chips back kind of mid October, November when we should have got them in, in August
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: ADC Chip Design with Anthony Wall

claims.claim_text: In regions without local supply the constraint on experimental work is planning horizon rather than money, since a needed item may be a month away and inspiration-driven work cannot wait that long.
claims.quote_verbatim: it might be a month before they get that thing they need
claims.speaker: Greg Gage
claims.episode_title: An interview with Greg and Tim of Backyard Brains - Boethetic Bug Brainwaves

claims.claim_text: On space hardware lead times are usually not the binding constraint, because parts are selected for suitability regardless of unit cost and are consequently already stocked at distributors.
claims.quote_verbatim: with that sort of project, lead times usually aren't too much of an issue either
claims.speaker: Jon Oxer

claims.claim_text: Early-stage companies routinely underestimate manufacturing intervals, and an eight-week lead time discovered late is enough to undo a plan built without one.
claims.quote_verbatim: eight week lead times are going to like, you know, shoot me in the foot
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Boeing, PCBs & Startups - Awful Airplane Aeration

claims.claim_text: The common requirement is a fully featured four-layer board with solder mask, silkscreen and plated-through holes within about a week; sub-day in-house turnaround answers a narrow set of needs rather than a general one.
claims.quote_verbatim: Most people are happy to wait a week to get their, you know, four-layer, silkscreen, solder mask, plate-through, you know, routed PCB.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Around 2011 a double-sided prototype board from a quick-turn fabricator ran about ninety dollars delivered in three or four days.
claims.quote_verbatim: But you get it in like three or four days.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Quoted manufacturing time is a ceiling rather than an estimate at some fabricators: a five to seven day quote was met in about two days before the shipping notice was issued.
claims.quote_verbatim: They said it would be six to seven days, five, five to seven days manufacturing time.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
